source.title: Task Ambiguity in Humans and Language Models
source.authors: Alex Tamkin; Kunal Handa; Ava Shrestha; Noah D. Goodman

record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model task accuracy across model sizes and training types, bearing conceptually on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are task-accuracy comparisons across language models. The paper does not test power-law loss scaling, extrapolation of loss, compute-optimal allocations, or architecture-shape effects. Values in Figures 2 and 3 are not given numerically in the text; cited scaling-law findings are not study results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates OpenAI models of several sizes, with and without HFD, on a new benchmark (AmbiBench). Its accuracy comparisons across model size bear only weakly on V6. They show downstream accuracy is not monotone in parameter count for base models, and size helps mainly with HFD. There is no loss measurement and no fitted law.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that combining scale (to 175B) with human-feedback training lets models approach or exceed human accuracy, while neither alone suffices. They add that finetuning davinci on a few ambiguous in-context examples closes the gap to HFD models; finetuning on unambiguous control examples does not.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates task accuracy on an ambiguity benchmark across existing models and training types; it does not fit held-out-loss power laws or run a controlled scaling sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Task-accuracy outcomes differ by model size and HFD training; the paper also reports sensitivity to prompt format for t0pp, though that result is not about the scaling-law versions tested here.
record.problems: The evidence for V6 is task-specific and largely described qualitatively in the text; the relevant figure values are not stated numerically. Model comparisons do not isolate parameter count from training data or training method, and several model parameter counts are undisclosed.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-relevant results were reported in a form that bears on V6. Other reported experiments, including fine-tuning on ambiguous examples, measure an intervention on task ambiguity rather than performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Relation of downstream accuracy to pretraining loss; any quantitative prediction of accuracy from scale. HFD model sizes are undisclosed, and size is confounded with training data and method.

missing.what: Scale ordering within HFD models: text-davinci-002/003 strongly outperform text-curie-001, text-babbage-001 and text-ada-001.
Scale ordering within base models: curie and j1-jumbo beat the other OpenAI base models; davinci is no better; T0++ (11B) is near chance on Q/A.
Statement that smaller models perform worse, though all produce valid outputs by the end of the episode.

record.verdict_notes: Weak bearing on V6: the study evaluates commercial models at a few sizes, and HFD model sizes are undisclosed. No accuracy numbers appear in the text; the evidence is qualitative and drawn from figures. Reader rows R1 and R3–R6 are human or training-type comparisons and were unlinked from V6.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' held-out loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute grows.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures AmbiBench task accuracy, not downstream benchmark performance generally; it does not relate accuracy to pretraining loss or establish a quantitative predictive law.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, and whether curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: text-davinci-002
rows.size_stated: not stated; Appendix E says HFD model parameter counts have not been released
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated task disambiguation accuracy as the number of labeled in-context examples increased.

conditions.value: Arrow and Q/A; performance reported averaged across formats

rows.value: The best language model, text-davinci-002, significantly outperformed human participants.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown in Figure 3; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: The textual result is qualitative; no accuracy values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Compares text-davinci-002 with humans, not across scale. It does not measure V6's scale relation.

rows.subject: curie
rows.operation_detail: Compared task disambiguation accuracy across the example-count curve with the larger davinci model.
rows.baseline: davinci, stated as larger; 175B parameters in Appendix E
rows.value: The smaller curie model reliably outperformed davinci across the examples.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown in Figure 3; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: The stated comparison runs counter to a simple expectation that the larger model performs better.
rows.check: Correctly linked: curie (6.7B) reliably beats davinci (175B) on multi-example disambiguation (Fig. 3 caption).

rows.subject: text-curie-001
rows.size_stated: not stated; Appendix E says HFD model parameter counts have not been released
rows.operation_detail: Compared task accuracy at curie scale for HFD and non-HFD models.
rows.measure: Task accuracy as the number of examples grows
rows.value: The paper states that HFD training hurts at curie scale.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown in Figure 3; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: This is a comparison of training types at the same stated model scale, not a controlled parameter-count sweep.
rows.check: Compares HFD with non-HFD at the same curie scale, which is a training-type comparison, not a scale effect. The scale×HFD interaction belongs in a missing row.

rows.subject: text-davinci-002
rows.size_stated: not stated; Appendix E says HFD model parameter counts have not been released
rows.operation_detail: Compared task accuracy at davinci scale for HFD and non-HFD models.
rows.measure: Task accuracy as the number of examples grows
rows.value: The paper states that HFD dramatically helps at davinci scale.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown in Figure 3; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: The result indicates that training type changes the relationship between model scale and task accuracy.
rows.check: Compares HFD with non-HFD at davinci scale, which is a training-type comparison, not a scale effect.

rows.subject: davinci
rows.stage_stated: normal language model; not trained with HFD
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated accuracy when disambiguating tasks from informative natural-language instructions.

conditions.value: two labeled examples and one query

rows.baseline: Humans performed perfectly in all but one task
rows.value: The non-HFD 175B+ parameter davinci model performed relatively poorly.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown in Figure 2; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: The paper explicitly says the large non-HFD model did not match the strong human result.
rows.check: Baseline is humans, not smaller models. The text says all non-HFD models do poorly, so no scale trend is readable from this row.

rows.subject: text-davinci-003
rows.size_stated: not stated; Appendix E says HFD model parameter counts have not been released
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated accuracy when disambiguating tasks from natural-language instructions.

conditions.value: two labeled examples and one query

rows.value: The text-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003 HFD models closely followed human performance; the best HFD model, text-davinci-003, approached human accuracy for both instruction levels.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown in Figure 2; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: The paper reports near-human rather than uniformly perfect performance.
rows.check: Compares HFD davinci models with humans, not across scale.

relationships.condition: Non-HFD OpenAI base models, multi-example AmbiBench disambiguation
relationships.reason: The 6.7B curie reliably outperforms the 175B davinci across 1–20 examples, so accuracy does not rise with scale (R2).
relationships.display_finding: The 6.7B curie model reliably outperformed the 175B davinci model across 1–20 examples.

relationships.condition: Across training types (HFD vs base), both AmbiBench settings
relationships.reason: Based on the text, since no rows capture it: larger HFD models (text-davinci-00x) beat smaller HFD models. Among base models, scale gives no reliable gain, and HFD hurts at curie but helps at davinci.
relationships.display_finding: Larger HFD models outperformed smaller HFD models, base models showed no reliable scaling gain, and HFD hurt curie but helped davinci.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Across the multiple-example AmbiBench comparison of curie and davinci
reader_labels.reason: The smaller curie model reliably outperformed the larger davinci model, contrary to a simple predictable improvement with scale (R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: AmbiBench accuracy across model training types and instruction conditions
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy depends on training type: HFD hurts at curie scale but helps at davinci scale; the large non-HFD davinci model performs relatively poorly, while HFD davinci models approach human performance (R3, R4, R5, R6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The strongest tested HFD model significantly outperformed human participants as the number of examples increased (R1).
